title: WHO TOLD YOU?
paragraphs:
WHO TOLD YOU?
The Question God Asked in Eden That Still Exposes the Voice Behind Your Shame—and Leads You From Hiding to the Grace of Jesus Christ
There are questions God asks in Scripture that seem almost too simple to frighten us.
“Where are you?”
“Why are you afraid?”
“Do you want to be made well?”
“Who do you say that I am?”
But buried inside the wreckage of humanity’s first sin is another question.
Four words in English.
A question God asked a naked man hiding among trees.
A question that has followed humanity ever since.
“Who told you?”
Not merely, “What happened?”
Not merely, “What did you do?”
But...
Who told you?
And perhaps you have never realized how close that question can come to your own heart.
Who told you that because you failed again, God could never want you?
Who told you that your worst night became your permanent identity?
Who told you that what somebody did to you determined your worth?

Who told you that because your marriage failed, your ministry collapsed, your child wandered, your addiction returned, your secret became public, your prayers grew weak, or your past became ugly, you were now beyond redemption?
Who told you that you had to hide from the God who already knew where you were?
Go back to Eden.
Before the hiding.
Before the blame.
Before the shame.
Before the leaves.
Before humanity learned to look at itself through the fractured lens of sin.
Genesis describes the man and woman as naked and unashamed. Then the serpent entered the conversation.
That detail matters.
The catastrophe of Genesis 3 did not begin with Adam and Eve suddenly deciding that fruit looked delicious.
It began with a voice challenging the Word and character of God.
“Did God actually say...?”
The serpent attacked trust before the humans committed the act.
God had spoken.
Then another voice interpreted God.
That pattern has never disappeared.
God speaks, and another voice whispers, Can you really trust Him?
God establishes truth, and another voice asks, Is that really what He meant?
God gives boundaries for life, and another voice suggests those boundaries are evidence that God is withholding something good.
The serpent did not need Eve to stop believing in God altogether.
He only needed her to begin distrusting the God she believed in.
Then came the fruit.
Then came the fall.
Then came the terrible awakening.
Genesis 3:7 says their eyes were opened and they knew they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together and made coverings for themselves.
Humanity had just sinned, and almost immediately humanity became a tailor.
Think about that.
We have been sewing fig leaves ever since.
Achievement can become a fig leaf.
Religion can become a fig leaf.
Money can become a fig leaf.
A carefully maintained reputation can become a fig leaf.
Posting smiling family photographs while everyone inside the house is breaking can become a fig leaf.
Knowing Christian vocabulary while secretly living far from Christ can become a fig leaf.
Serving in church can even become a fig leaf when ministry is being used to conceal a heart that refuses to surrender.
We hide behind humor.
We hide behind anger.
We hide behind busyness.
We hide behind theology.
We hide behind “I’m fine.”
And sometimes we become so skilled at covering ourselves that everybody believes us.
Except God.
Then Adam heard the sound of the LORD God in the garden.
And he hid.
The creature hid from his Creator among the Creator’s trees.
It is tragic.
And painfully familiar.
Because sin still makes people do irrational things.
We hide from the One who sees everything.
We avoid prayer because we sinned, although prayer is exactly where confession should take us.
We avoid Scripture because Scripture exposes us, although the Word is exactly what we need.
We distance ourselves from Christian community because we are ashamed, although isolation often gives temptation more room to breathe.
Then God called to Adam:
“Where are you?”
God was not geographically confused.
Adam was lost.
God was not asking for coordinates. He was confronting Adam relationally and morally, drawing the hiding man into the light.
Adam answered that he heard God, became afraid because he was naked, and hid.
Then comes Genesis 3:11.
Read the Hebrew slowly:
מִי הִגִּיד לְךָ כִּי עֵירֹם אָתָּה
Mi higgid lekha ki ‘erom attah?
“Who told you that you were naked?”
The Hebrew מִי — mi means “who.”
הִגִּיד — higgid carries the straightforward sense of “told,” “declared,” or “made known.”
לְךָ — lekha means “to you.”
עֵירֹם — ‘erom means “naked.”
So we should resist turning the Hebrew into something mystical that the text itself does not say. God’s question is followed immediately by another:
“Have you eaten from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat?”
That second question keeps the first one anchored in its context.
God is exposing Adam’s disobedience.
This is not merely a motivational passage about ignoring negative opinions. It is not biblical permission to dismiss every uncomfortable voice by saying, “That isn’t from God.”
Sometimes the uncomfortable voice is Scripture.
Sometimes conviction hurts.
Sometimes God tells us something about ourselves that we desperately need to hear.
The deeper point is not, “Never listen to anyone who makes you feel bad.”
The point is that Adam’s newly experienced shame and hiding revealed that something catastrophic had happened in his relationship with God.
He had crossed the boundary God explicitly gave him.
The ancient Greek translation of Genesis, the Septuagint, preserves the question similarly:
τίς ἀνήγγειλέν σοι ὅτι γυμνὸς εἶ
τίς — tis means “who.”
ἀνήγγειλέν — anēngeilen means “reported,” “announced,” or “told.”
σοι — soi means “to you.”
γυμνὸς — gymnos means “naked.”
The question survives translation because the confrontation is unmistakable:
Who told you?
Yet notice something extraordinary.
God knew.
God knew about the serpent.
God knew about the fruit.
God knew about the disobedience.
God knew why Adam was hiding.
The question was not God collecting information.
It was God bringing a sinner into confession.
That distinction changes everything.
When God confronts us, He does not do so because our confession will finally update heaven’s database.
You cannot shock an omniscient God.
There is no sentence beginning with “God, I need to tell You something...” that ends with God saying, “I had no idea.”
He knows.
He knows what happened when nobody was watching.
He knows the browser history.
He knows the private messages.
He knows the bitterness behind the smile.
He knows what happened in the hotel room.
He knows what you did with the money.
He knows why you stopped praying.
He knows what you secretly envy.
He knows the resentment you rehearse at night.
He knows the habit you promised would never happen again.
He knows the part of your testimony you conveniently leave out.
And still He calls sinners out of hiding.
That is what makes Eden so devastating and so beautiful.
Adam had sinned.
God came looking.
Adam hid.
God called.
Adam confessed only partially.
Then Adam blamed.
“The woman whom You gave to be with me...”
Listen carefully to that sentence.
Sin rarely remains content simply to disobey God.
It starts rewriting responsibility.
Adam effectively points toward Eve—and ultimately toward God who gave Eve to him.
Eve then points toward the serpent.
Human beings have been pointing ever since.
My parents.
My spouse.
My childhood.
My church.
My boss.
My loneliness.
My trauma.
My friends.
My circumstances.
Those things can genuinely wound us, influence us, tempt us, and help explain our struggles. Compassion requires acknowledging that.
But explanation cannot become absolution for our own sin.
The Gospel does not heal us by teaching us to blame better.
It heals us by bringing us into truth.
There is an enormous difference between shame and biblical conviction.
Shame says, “Hide.”
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “There is no hope for someone like you.”
The Gospel says that for those who are in Christ Jesus there is no condemnation.
Shame wants your sin concealed.
Grace brings your sin to a Savior.
And this is where “Who told you?” becomes dangerously personal.
Because some of us have allowed voices other than God’s Word to become interpreters of our identity.
Someone abandoned you, and somewhere inside you a sentence formed:
I am unlovable.
Someone abused you, and shame whispered:
I am dirty.
You failed publicly:
I am finished.
You fell into the same temptation again:
God must be tired of me.
Someone chose somebody else:
I was never enough.
Your prayers seem unanswered:
God has forgotten me.
You look at somebody else’s life:
God loves them more.
You remember what you did ten years ago:
That is who I really am.
And God’s question cuts through the noise:
Who told you?
Not every thought that speaks in your own voice tells the truth.
Not every feeling deserves authority.
Not every accusation deserves agreement.
Not every label deserves residence in your soul.
But neither should we answer God’s question with cheap positive thinking.
The biblical answer to shame is not standing in front of a mirror repeating, “I’m amazing.”
The biblical answer is much stronger.
We really have sinned.
We really are guilty.
We really cannot save ourselves.
And God really has provided a Savior.
Christianity does not rescue you by pretending the scandal never happened.
It announces that grace can rewrite what sin tried to make final.
Look again at Eden.
Judgment is pronounced. Sin has consequences. Death enters the human story.
But in the middle of judgment comes a promise.
Genesis 3:15 speaks of the offspring of the woman who will ultimately crush the serpent’s head while Himself being wounded.

Christians have long recognized here the earliest biblical anticipation of the Gospel—the first glimmer of the coming victory that unfolds across Scripture and reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Before Adam and Eve leave Eden, something else happens.
Genesis 3:21 says:
וַיַּעַשׂ יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים לְאָדָם וּלְאִשְׁתּוֹ כָּתְנוֹת עוֹר וַיַּלְבִּשֵׁם
The LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife...
וַיַּלְבִּשֵׁם — wayyalbishem
“And He clothed them.”
Do not rush past that.
They made coverings.
God clothed them.
Their coverings were inadequate.
God provided what they could not provide for themselves.

We should be careful not to claim more than Genesis explicitly states. The text does not directly explain how the skins were obtained or explicitly call this an atoning sacrifice. But within the larger biblical story, the scene powerfully anticipates a recurring reality: sinful humanity cannot ultimately solve guilt and shame through self-made coverings. God must provide what sinners cannot.
And eventually, He does so fully in Christ.
Not fig leaves.
Not reputation.
Not religious performance.
Not pretending.
Jesus.
At the cross, the scandal becomes almost unbearable.
The sinless Son of God is publicly humiliated.
Stripped.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Wounded.
Crucified.
He bears sin, though He Himself is without sin.
And here the Gospel becomes more than inspirational language.
Paul writes that God made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
Peter says Christ Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree.
Isaiah, centuries earlier, speaks of the Servant wounded for our transgressions.
Jesus does not merely tell ashamed sinners to feel better about themselves.
He deals with the reason sinners should fear judgment.
He deals with sin.
The cross says your sin is more serious than your excuses have admitted...
and God’s grace is greater than your shame has imagined.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Redemption.
Not “You never did anything wrong.”
Forgiveness.
Not “Sin does not matter.”
A cross demonstrating exactly how much it matters.
Not “Stay as you are.”
Repent, believe, receive mercy, and follow Jesus.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe beneath everything people know about you, there is something they do not know.
A room in your heart you keep locked.
A memory you cannot erase.
A habit you cannot seem to kill.
A wound that distorted how you see yourself.
A sin you have renamed because calling it sin would require repentance.
A version of yourself you work very hard to keep everyone from meeting.
And perhaps you have spent years sewing leaves.
Jesus is not asking you to sew faster.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent of what needs abandoning.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek reconciliation where it is biblically possible and wise.
Ask for help when you cannot fight alone.
Stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Stop calling compromise “complicated.”
Stop calling hiding “privacy” when what you really fear is exposure.
But also stop calling yourself something Jesus has not called the repentant sinner who belongs to Him.
If you are in Christ, your sin may be part of your history.
It does not get to be your lord.
Your wound may explain part of your story.
It does not get to write the ending.
Your failure may have consequences.
It does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus.
This is the Gospel’s breathtaking reversal:
We hide because we are ashamed.
God calls us out.
We expect only judgment.
God points toward redemption.
We try to cover ourselves.
God provides the covering.
We run from Him.
Christ comes for sinners.
We deserve death.
Christ dies.
Christ rises.
And everyone who repents and trusts in Him receives something Adam’s fig leaves could never manufacture:
reconciliation with God.
That is why the question still matters.
Who told you?
Who told you Jesus cannot forgive that?
Who told you repentance means God will reject you?
Who told you confession is the end of your story?
Who told you the prodigal cannot come home?
Who told you the sexually broken cannot become holy?
Who told you the addict cannot become free?
Who told you the bitter cannot learn forgiveness?
Who told you the lukewarm cannot wake up?
Who told you the wounded cannot heal?
Who told you the fallen believer should simply stay on the ground?
Scripture does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears when we repent.
It promises something infinitely better.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is reconciliation with God through Christ.
There is new life in Christ.
There is transformation by the Spirit of Christ.
There is resurrection hope because Christ walked out of His grave.
Your answer to shame is not a better opinion of yourself.
Your answer is Jesus Christ.
Maybe you know someone hiding right now.
You can see it in them.
The smile is there, but something behind their eyes is exhausted.
They still say, “God is good,” but privately they wonder whether He could still be good to them.
And if this exposed something in you, do not disappear quietly.
Your comment may become the sentence another ashamed believer reads and realizes, I am not the only person fighting.
Not because every sentence is easy.
There may be a night when shame remembers your address.
When that happens, come back—not merely to these words, but to the Scriptures behind them.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as a way to purchase God’s favor, prove that you love God, or earn spiritual blessing. Salvation is by grace, and generosity must never be manipulated.

But if you genuinely desire to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, supporting faithful Gospel work is one practical way your generosity can help truth travel farther. Pray for the ministry because nothing of eternal value happens apart from God.
If you are ready to support the mission and go deeper:
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Christ paid the price sinners could never pay.
So before you leave, return once more to the garden.
See Adam hiding.
See the leaves.
Hear God walking toward the fugitive.
Listen.
“Where are you?”
Then hear Adam confess his fear.
And finally...
“Who told you that you were naked?”
Thousands of years later, humanity is still hiding.
Different gardens.
Different leaves.
Different scandals.
Same desperate need.
But now we know where the story was going.
From Eden to Bethlehem.
From Bethlehem to Golgotha.
From Golgotha to an empty tomb.
From our scandal...
to His grace.
So when shame whispers your old name tonight, do not answer it with another fig leaf.
Answer by running to Jesus.

Because the voice that exposed Adam’s hiding in the garden became the Gospel invitation calling sinners out of darkness—and the hands that sinners could never cleanse themselves were answered by nail-scarred hands strong enough to bring them home.
